Lisavu, an island that lives on import taxes, values everything landed, with freight and insurance to the island. Every declaration follows the rule of the country it is lodged in, and a customs value declared on a transport document agrees with it; so the same bench has one customs value entering Bayvarra and another entering Lisavu.

section.title: Money and payment
section.para: The three currencies trade at fixed parities: 1 lume = 100 ferra = 0.4 coral. The coral has been tied to the lume since the Lumeport Agreement of 1974, as an island that sells its cotton in lume has every reason to do; the ferra joined at a fixed parity when the Trade Accord came into force in 1996. The parities are fixed by the Accord's monetary protocol and reviewed every five years, against how the three economies have developed: an adjustable peg, as the Bretton Woods system was. The last review, on 1 January 2022, left them unchanged; the next is on 1 January 2027. Through 2026 every exchange rate in the examples is the parity. There is still a daily official rate, the noon fixing of the Lumeport Exchange, which between the three currencies does not change between reviews, and the Accord's size classes give their turnover limits in all three currencies at the parities. Currency risk is real across a review: anything agreed now and paid after 1 January 2027 may be paid at another rate, and a forward exchange contract protects a long commitment across the review date.

Against currencies outside the Accord the lume floats. Its value is a basket of fixed amounts of five currencies, like the IMF's SDR: the Swiss franc, the Canadian dollar, the Australian dollar, the Norwegian krone and the Mexican peso, weighted 30, 25, 15, 15 and 15 % when the basket was set, on 2 January 2026, at 1.20 lume to the euro. Every working day at noon the Lumeport Exchange publishes its fixing of the lume against eight currencies: the euro, the US dollar, the yen, the Indian rupee, the pound sterling, the yuan, the rand and the real. The ferra's and the coral's rates against them follow from the parities, which stay fixed inside the Accord.

A party keeps its account at a bank of its own country, with one exception. For its framework contract with the Lumeport Public Works Department Valdara holds a lume account at Bank of Lumeport, the bank that gave its tender guarantee: its invoices under the contract ask for payment in lume into that account, so the department pays its own currency to a domestic account, and its remittance advice is in lume throughout. Valdara converts the lume into ferra later if it wants, its currency risk across the review covered by a forward contract with its bank; a conversion is the banks' business and shows on the bank statement, not in the payer's remittance. Its value added tax stays in ferra, its tax currency.

Payment terms come in three layers. First, what the parties agreed in a contract or a framework agreement. Where they agreed nothing, the seller's standard terms, which follow its country's practice: Urvania gives 2 % discount for payment within ten days of 30 days net; Bayvarra charges a surcharge per month late on 30 days net; the island gives 45 days. Where neither says anything about late payment, the statutory interest of the seller's country applies: in Urvania 8 % a year, in Bayvarra 7 %, one federal rate under its federal commercial law, and on the island 6 %; so a utility bill, whose Accord term says nothing on late payment, carries it. Across a border the seller's country's rule applies, unless the contract chooses another. So Valdara's framework agreement with its rail carrier sets 30 days net from the consignment note, and the carrier's invoices fall due from the consignment note with no discount; the public works contract sets 30 days after each accepted release, so Valdara's invoice falls due from the acceptance, not from its own date. A standard terms code means one text and one period wherever it is used.

Utility bills are due 21 days after they are issued, in all three countries, by a rule of the Accord, part of the common minimum it sets for the customers of the national utilities. They carry terms of their own, an Accord code, TA-UTIL, not a country's standard terms; a bill collected by direct debit says so and is collected on the due date.

A utility gives each customer a customer number of its own; the supply contract keeps its own number. The statement behind a bill shows, beside the utility's own supply, the part of the bill another party really supplies: in Urvania Ferrano Grid's network charges, which Ferrano Energy collects with its bill and pays to the grid (its tariff of 27.3 ferra a kilowatt hour is 21.1 for the energy and 6.2 for the network), and in Bayvarra the city's sewage levy, which the water company collects for the city. The island's telephone company bills its own service only.

A business with a meter read monthly is billed every month on its reading. A household pays on account: each April the utility estimates the year, and a twelfth of it, rounded up to a whole lume, is collected every month by direct debit. The meters are read once a year, at the end of March; the annual statement and the settlement bill charge the actual year less what was paid, and the new estimate sets the next year's monthly amount. In Lumeport the water company also runs the district heating, so a household on the network has one annual account for water, the city's levy and heat, with a cooling correction per megawatt hour when the return water comes back too warm. Water is exempt from the sales tax, the levy is outside it, and the heat carries the state's sales tax like any sale to a consumer.

Bayvarra rounds cash payments to 5 cents, its smallest coin. A transfer quotes a creditor reference in the structure of ISO 11649, made from the invoice number, so the payee can match it, and runs over the domestic clearing or, between the countries, the trade accord's payment link. Coral net, the island's clearing, settles tokenised deposits on the Bank of Selanu's ledger.

section.title: Prices
section.para: Prices along the bench's chain follow its steps, and the figures are a current base. Valdara has a list price, the price of its list VI-PL-2026, which a direct customer pays, and gives Lumeway, its distributor for Bayvarra and the island under a distribution agreement of 1996, a lower distributor price: it sells the bench to Lumeway at 399.00 lume, and to the public works department, delivered, at its list price of 499.00, which the tender catalogue calls the contract price. Lumeway sells it to the department store and to the island's importer at a trade price of 520.00, a margin of about 22 % after the truck from Ferrano. The store sells it to a shopper at a shop price of 749.00, or 674.10 in the two weeks of 10 % off when its home and garden department reopens after a renovation on 11 May. On the island Velumi Trading sells it in its Selanu shop at 375 coral (937.50 lume): after the CIF price, the import consumption tax of 10 % and its clearance, about 38 %, a retailer's margin. The spare side frame goes from Valdara to Lumeway at 47.50; Lumeway's trade price for it is 64.00, and 58.00 on its revised list of 20 May. To the island Lumeway sells it at 68.00, CIF Selanu: a price with the frame's share of the container haulage to the port, the sea freight, export clearance and insurance in it, which leaves Lumeway about 16 %. Under CIF the prices hold the freight and the insurance: Lumeway pays its forwarder for them and bills the island's buyer the goods alone. The cargo insurance that CIF obliges Lumeway to take out costs a premium of 0.22 % of the insured value, the CIF value plus 10 %, so it follows the value of each shipment. The eight urgent frames that fly to the island go at the trade price, carriage paid to Selanu airport, and Lumeway recharges the air freight at cost, a surcharge the island's buyer accepted when it asked for them. In the public tender Valdara bids 499 a bench plus 18 for installation: above what its distributor pays and below what its distributor charges, a direct project price.

A shop price in Bayvarra excludes the sales tax, which is added at the till (674.10, tax 43.82 at 6.5 %, 717.92 to pay): the tax is levied once, at the final sale, by the state. On the island there is no sales tax, so the price is the price. With its value added tax, a consumer price in Urvania would include the tax. Every kind of price in the world's price type list (trade, distributor, catalogue, contract, recommended retail, promotional price) is a price before tax, and the list says so for each.

Three rules of thumb keep the figures plausible, and the build checks them: nobody resells below what they paid plus the freight the documents state (shared over a transport's load by gross weight) and the import tax they bear; a reseller's gross margin falls in a band for its kind (a distributor 15 to 30 %, a retailer 30 to 45 %, and 40 to 60 % on clothing, lower during a promotion), freight recharged at cost counting neither as cost nor as price; and a company's turnover per person falls in a band for its kind.

section.title: Document numbers
section.para: Every issuer numbers its own documents, per kind of document, and its numbers rise with the time of issue across all flows. The numbers reflect the size of the business: the examples show a sample of each company's sequence, with gaps where its other business lies. A distributor that issues some 2,800 invoices a year is near number 920 at the end of April; a farm is in its low two digits.

The style of a number fits the issuer's country, size and trade. Large companies use plain numeric ranges from their business systems, one range per kind of document, running on from year to year (4500021873). Mid-sized companies use a code of their own, the kind of document, the year and a number, restarting each year (LMW-INV-26-0920); each company chooses its code, which is unique in the world and not made from its initials. Small companies write the year and a number. Public bodies use file references (PWD/2026/0187). In Urvania invoices and credit notes are numbered within the year by its rules for value added tax (2026/0920), whatever the seller's own style; Bayvarra and Lisavu have no such rule. Transport documents follow their trade: an air waybill has the airline's three-digit prefix, a serial and a check digit, a bill of lading the shipping line's code and a number, a utility bill the customer's account and the period. Whoever runs the system gives the number: a shopper's web order carries the shop's number. Which issuer uses which style is a current base.
A number says nothing by itself: what a document is, and who issued it, is said by its elements. A creditor reference on an invoice is built from the invoice number and changes with it.

A transaction has an identifier of its own. ProfileExecutionID identifies one collaboration: one run of a process between the same parties, such as an order with its despatch advice and its invoice, or a tender procedure. The party that starts the collaboration gives it, in its own numbering style (for an order-to-invoice cycle the buyer, for a tender the contracting body, whose procurement file is such an identifier), and every later document of that transaction repeats it, so that a reader can collect the documents of one transaction by this element alone. A document that belongs to no collaboration with others carries none.

section.title: The calendar
section.para: Offices and factories work Monday to Friday; shops Monday to Saturday; ports, carriers, terminals, border customs and the operations of utilities every day, and their contacts say so. The week is the same in all three countries. A document is dated on a day its issuer works, unless it says why not, and the build checks it.

The three states are secular: there is no state church and the law names no religion. The public holidays fall on dates a reader recognises and carry civil names, as Uruguay's did when it renamed its holidays in 1919. The seasons are those of the south: December is midsummer and August midwinter, and the island's cotton is picked from March to May. All three countries keep 1 January as New Year's Day and Accord Day, the day the Trade Accord came into force in 1996. The holidays below, with their dates in 2026, are a current base.
Urvania has 11 days, on fixed dates, in the Italian manner; a holiday that falls on a weekend is not made up for.

section.para: The countries are not kept in step. On 1 May Urvania and the island are closed and Bayvarra works; on Monday 4 May it is the other way round. On Upland State Day Marrowdale is closed and Lumeport is open. An order sent on the receiver's holiday is read a day later; a due date on a holiday moves to the next working day; a payment between two countries settles on a day both banking systems are open; a deadline in working days counts the working days of the party that set it. Ports, ships, aircraft and border customs work through all of it, and those who plan a ship's arrival plan around such days.

The world has two time zones and no summer time. The mainland is one hour behind UTC (UTC−01:00) and the island on UTC (UTC+00:00), all year. Each country names its own legal time: Urvanian Time and Bayvarran Time, both UTC−01:00, and Lisavu Time, UTC+00:00. Documents use no abbreviations, which are not standardised and collide, and not "GMT", the name of the United Kingdom's civil time. A time is written with its offset from UTC, as ISO 8601 writes it (07:00:00-01:00), at least wherever a document crosses the zone boundary, and an address states its zone as an offset. A flight that leaves Lumeport at 07:00 is timetabled into Selanu at 10:45 island time: a block time of 2 h 45, of which about 2 h 10 to 2 h 15 are needed eastbound with the westerly winds, so it usually lands early.

The week starts on Monday in all three countries, and weeks are numbered as ISO 8601 numbers them: week 1 is the week with the year's first Thursday. In 2026 week 1 runs from Monday 29 December 2025 to Sunday 4 January 2026, and the year has 53 weeks. UBL has no element for a week number, so a document states a week as a period from Monday to Sunday, described by the code WEEK of the world's period list; a week number appears only in free text ("delivery in week 21"), and then as the ISO number.

section.title: Flows of documents
section.para: The parties do business in flows. Each country has its own raw material and industry: Urvania mines ore and makes park benches, recovering its production waste as recycled plastic; Bayvarra saws timber, makes furniture, packaging and clothing, and distributes and retails; the island Lisavu grows and gins cotton, its export. Goods cross the land border by road, rail and river barge and go overseas by sea and air in both directions; there is a public tender and a design contest, a temporary export with an ATA carnet, a utility in each country, gas by pipeline from Bayvarra's offshore field to Urvania's power station and grid, and propane by road tanker from the gas plant to Lumeport's district heating. Each flow starts from the business: who buys from whom, on which delivery terms, and therefore who arranges and pays the transport. A distributor that buys free carrier (FCA) books the truck itself and names the carrier in its order; a retailer that buys delivered duty paid (DDP) leaves the transport to its supplier, who then needs an outgoing waybill.

A document that is revised keeps its number and says which version it supersedes, with VersionID 2 and PreviousVersionID 1, and its note says what changed. The design contest shows this: the city of Lumeport relaunches a contest for its harbour promenade bench, cancelled the year before because no design met the brief (the new notice gives the reason), offers three prizes and asks a group of designers to form a limited company before the follow-up contract. Its notices are design-contest notices, after the eForms notice types cn-desg and can-desg. The council raises the prize fund and with it the estimate (the prizes and the follow-up design contract of about 40,000 lume), a corrigendum corrects the site plan, extends the deadline for requests and lets an industrial designer lead a design, and the design team of Brackenmere Furniture and Saltmere Engineering updates its declarations: Brackenmere's own designer takes the lead from Saltmere's architect. The team's references are the reading garden of Lumeport's central library and the promenade benches on Larkmouth's seafront. The registry checks both members and reissues Brackenmere's extract when new accounts are filed; a small design studio is excluded at the selection for unpaid social security contributions. The jury gives the first prize to the team, the second to Valdara and withholds the third, and the results notice corrects the first prize, which its first version gave as the amount first planned.
Every document in a flow records:

listitem.para: the document type, its sender and its receiver;
why it is sent, in business terms;
every party it mentions, at its place in the UBL structure, for example the road carrier at Order/Delivery/Despatch/CarrierParty.

section.para: A flow also lists its transport legs: the mode, from which party to which, and the carrier. The goods only move where the world allows it. A road leg needs a road from party to party, so a truck cannot drive to the island; a rail leg needs a rail line between them, a barge needs the river at both ends, gas a pipeline from party to party, a ship a sea route from port to port and an aircraft an air route from airport to airport. The carrier must have a vehicle, train, vessel, aircraft or pipeline of that mode in its fleet, and every carrier a document of the flow names must carry one of its legs. Domestic jobs go to a carrier of that country: a truck of one country driving within another would be cabotage, which only happens where a document says so.

A truck is weighed against the Trade Accord's road protocol: a tractor unit with its semi-trailer, or a truck with its trailer, may weigh at most 40 tonnes with its load. The carrier's fleet gives each vehicle's empty weight, so its payload is what is left: Trasvia's tractor of about 7.8 t and its curtain-side trailer of about 7.5 t can carry about 24.7 t. A weighed load stays within both, and the build checks it.

Dangerous goods by road follow the ADR, which the Accord's road rules apply also to a carriage within one country. Kelpstone Gas separates propane from its field's gas at the Gullhaven plant and sells it by road tanker; in winter the Coastal State Water Company burns it in the peak boilers of Lumeport's district heating and orders a tanker load when its storage runs low. Gullhaven Tank Haulage, a tank haulier beside the plant with the federal permit to carry dangerous goods in tanks, carries it: about 20 t of propane, UN 1965, hydrocarbon gas mixture, liquefied, n.o.s., mixture C, of class 2.1, in a tank semi-trailer that weighs about 17 t with its tractor, so about 37 t and within the 40 t. The tank shows the class 2.1 placard and, front and back, the orange plates with the hazard identification number 23 (gas, flammable) over the UN number 1965; the consignment note gives the tunnel restriction code B/D, which forbids a tank of it every road tunnel (the road from Gullhaven to Lumeport has none), and the crew carries the Accord's emergency card for class 2. The tanker is weighed empty and full on the plant's weighbridge, which gives the tonnes billed, drives the day to Lumeport, about 515 km, pumps the propane into the water company's storage and returns empty the next day. Its consignment note reports the CO2e of both runs, loaded and empty, from the diesel each used, because the water company's greenhouse-gas report asks its suppliers' carriers for the whole round trip.

Waste that stays in Urvania moves under Urvania's own waste law, not under the Basel Convention's procedure for transboundary movements, on the model of a national reporting point for waste. Urvania's environment agency is the competent authority: it issues the permits of waste treatment plants, registers waste carriers, and receives two reports. The producer notifies its waste stream for a year before the first load (the waste by its code in Urvania's waste list, which takes over the numbers and the rules of the European List of Waste, the planned total, the number of loads, the period, the loading place and the facility), and the agency acknowledges it with a waste-stream number; a domestic stream of non-hazardous waste for recovery needs no consent. The facility then reports each load it receives, with its net weight from its weighbridge and the stream's number. UBL's waste notification requires a CustomsParty, "the competent authority granting a permit to export or import the waste"; for a domestic stream it names the environment agency, the only competent authority there is.

Goods that go abroad for a while and come back, such as samples for a fair, travel under an ATA carnet, which the Accord's countries take over from the real convention on temporary admission. The exporter's chamber of commerce issues it and guarantees it, the chamber of the country visited guarantees it there, and customs stamp its counterfoils as the goods move: exportation and re-importation at home, importation and re-exportation abroad, and a transit counterfoil with its two vouchers for each crossing of a third country, on entry and on exit. As issued, a carnet carries its counterfoils unstamped. Valdara shows two Serra benches at the Selanu Chamber of Commerce's trade fair in early June: the carnet is issued on 25 May, the samples cross Bayvarra on their transit vouchers both ways, and the island's customs give them until 30 June to leave. Its re-exportation voucher goes astray, so in July, after the limit, the island's chamber asks for proof, a month later it reminds, and Urvania's chamber answers with the stamped counterfoils and Urvania's record of the re-import. What was at stake is only the island's import consumption tax of 10 % on the declared value and the carnet's surcharge of 10 % of it, about 44 coral: benches of Accord origin owe no duty.
A leg takes the time its distance needs at the mode's usual speed. Where a document's timeline is longer than that, the extra time has a reason that is part of the world, before any date moves:

listitem.para: Lumeway's customs desk, which clears its imports, works on weekdays from 08:00 to 17:00, and its goods-in takes deliveries in the morning only, in slots booked a week ahead. A truck that reaches the border after the desk has closed waits there for the night, which is also the driver's rest, clears in the morning and is unloaded in its slot.
A train stops at the border station for a crew change, a brake test and a seal check, and leaves on its timetabled path; a shunting trip then places the wagons on the receiver's siding.
Selanu's pilots bring ships in by daylight only. A ship that arrives in the dark does not anchor; it waits under way and berths at first light.
The barge on the river sails by daylight only and is unloaded by the receiver's morning shift.

section.para: An air leg also says how the goods are loaded, and the build checks that the load fits the island airline's ATR 72-600F, as ATR's fact sheet gives it: at most 9,200 kg, 75 m³ and seven LD3 containers, each within its own maximum weight, and loose pieces that pass the 2.94 × 1.80 m cargo door into the aft bulk compartment. The sample benches, at 1.8 m, fly loose. Dangerous goods are stowed as the IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations ask. The mast flow's twelve lithium-ion battery modules, 27 kg each in their crates on a pallet, and its box of five 1-litre tins of coating stripper may fly on cargo aircraft only, the stripper because five litres in one package are more than a passenger aircraft may take of it; both go in LD3 containers with net doors at the front of the main deck, where the crew can reach them, with an empty position between them, because the stripper's flammable subsidiary label must not be stowed next to the batteries. The smoke detectors, an excepted package of class 7, need neither crew access nor segregation and fly in a closed container further aft. No container is cooled: batteries on a flight of under three hours in the island's winter need no temperature control. A subsidiary hazard has no emergency schedule of its own in the IMDG Code, which gives one per UN entry; the road rules give the crew's actions per hazard label, so the subsidiary hazard names the Accord's emergency card of its class.

The island's hospital gets its medicines by air too. Selanu General Hospital, a public body, orders from Quillmoor Pharma Distribution, a pharmaceutical wholesaler beside Lumeport airport that holds Bayvarra's wholesale licence and a licence for radioactive material: on Wednesday 10 June the vaccines for the island's winter influenza campaign, insulin, forty doses of a frozen varicella vaccine and next week's technetium generator for its nuclear medicine unit, carriage paid to Selanu airport. Quillmoor had bought the vaccines and the insulin in April from its maker in India, in rupees, and imported them in May; it calls off the generator from its maker in the Netherlands, in euro, on the day of the hospital's order. The generator is a molybdenum-99 column in a shielded housing of 20 GBq at its reference time, Sunday 21 June at noon, six days after delivery, as European makers pre-calibrate them; it flies from Amsterdam on the Saturday, lands at Lumeport on the Sunday evening, and Quillmoor declares it for import at once and fetches it into its warehouse. Mo-99 halves in 65.94 hours, so at 05:30 on Monday, when Quillmoor's own van hands the package to the cargo terminal, it holds about 96 GBq: the shipper's declaration gives 97 GBq as the maximum activity in transport. It is a Type A package (Mo-99 may fill one up to 600 GBq), UN 2915, not special form and not fissile, with a transport index of 1.5 and so a Category III-YELLOW label, though its surface rate of 0.30 mSv/h alone would allow II-YELLOW. UBL has no element for the activity, the category or the surface rate: the activity goes into the radioactive material's name, the category and the surface rate into the hazardous item's additional information. The generator has a shipper's declaration of its own, as radioactive material may share one with no other dangerous goods but dry ice that cools it; the dry ice of the varicella box, 6 kg under packing instruction 954, appears on the air waybill only. Both rules rest on secondary sources so far: the IATA regulations themselves have not been read. The forwarder's truck brings the airline's active temperature-controlled container, set to 5 °C and closed in Quillmoor's cold room at 04:00, and the dry-ice box to the terminal; the morning flight KXL207 leaves at 07:00 with the container on the main deck and the two boxes in the aft hold, the radioactive package as far from the crew as the aircraft allows. On the island the container's logger shows the temperature between 4.4 and 5.8 °C all the way; the terminal attaches its readings to its arrival report, and Tevaro Customs Brokers declares the import as the hospital's direct representative, in the hospital's name: no duty, and the import consumption tax exempt for medicines supplied to a public hospital. The hospital pharmacy's van fetches the goods.

A ship reports to the port before it arrives, with its security and health certificates. The ocean carrier's second feeder came under Bayvarra's flag in January: it sails with an interim security certificate, valid like a full one for its six months, and says that it is interim; it carries a sanitation control exemption certificate, which Bayvarra's port health office at Lumeport issues when an inspection finds no control measures needed; the first feeder carries a sanitation control certificate, as its inspection found pests in the galley stores. The security report lists the ship-to-ship activities of the last ten port calls, here a bunkering from the port's barge, with the measure the ship took.

Fresh food crosses to the island in a reefer, a container with its own refrigeration. In the southern autumn the island's fresh-produce wholesaler, Hafefo Fresh Produce in Selanu, which keeps a cold store by the port and supplies the island's shops, hotels and the hospital's kitchen, buys a 40-foot reefer of apples and pears from Harrowmead Fruit Growers, a cooperative of the fruit growers on the slopes above Harrowmead in the wetter west of Upland State: Gala and Packham's Triumph pears from the cooperative's cold store and Granny Smith picked that month, 1,120 cartons of 18 kg on 20 pallets, all graded Class I under the Trade Accord's marketing standard for fresh fruit, which follows the UNECE standards for apples and pears; each carton is marked with its class and its count, and whole fresh fruit carries no best-before date. The cooperative's stored pears are running short, so it accepts the order on a condition, three pallets of pears instead of four and a fifth of Granny Smith in their place, open until the Friday noon before the sailing, when it must book the reefer; the wholesaler agrees and takes the changed mix. It buys carriage and insurance paid to the port of Selanu (CIP), the term the ICC advises for goods in containers, with the cover on all risks that perishable fruit needs: the cooperative books the reefer through its forwarder, which has it pre-cooled, brings it to the packhouse, trucks it back to Lumeport on a generator set clipped to the chassis, declares the export and insures the fruit for 110 % of its value. The wholesaler's order asks only that the fruit travel chilled; the cooperative's booking turns that into the reefer's settings. Before loading, the Plant Health Service of Bayvarra's federal Department of Agriculture, the country's plant protection organisation under the IPPC, inspects the fruit at the packhouse, on the application the forwarder lodges for the cooperative, and certifies it free of codling moth and fire blight, the two pests the island, which has neither, keeps out. The reefer is set to 0.5 °C, within 0 to 1 °C, at about 90 % humidity, with its fresh-air vent partly open because the fruit breathes; it sails on Tidewell's Thursday sailing and is off Selanu on the Saturday evening, two days later. The wholesaler lodges its import declaration while the ship is at sea, so that the fruit is released on discharge on the Sunday; the reefer waits on the port's power in its reefer rack, at a day's charge collect from the consignee, until the 3PL takes it to the cold store on the Monday morning, where it is unloaded, the reefer's log is read and the pulp temperature measured. The wholesaler pays the invoice in lume on its due date, 30 days after the invoice, from its account at the Bank of Selanu, which changes its coral. The fruit pays the island's import consumption tax like any import: the island taxes imported food to encourage its own farms.

The vehicles on the map are these legs: one truck, train, barge, ship or aircraft per leg, travelling the way the build found for it, from the from-party to the to-party, and a leg flown the same way by the same carrier in several flows is one aircraft. Each makes a round trip: it waits at the from-party, travels out, waits at the to-party and travels back, and a leg and its return leg by the same carrier are one vehicle. An aircraft takes off and lands along the runway: it rolls along it, climbs out straight ahead over the approach zone, and joins the final approach in line with the runway of the airport it goes to. A pipeline has no vehicle: the gas is shown flowing from the field to the consumers. Pipelines follow the rules of real ones. They are buried, so they cross roads, rail lines and the river underneath, at right angles and in a straight line, never along them; they keep out of towns, and nothing is built or planted on their right of way. They start at the producer, at its offshore platform or as a branch of another pipeline, end at a customer, and carry exactly the pipeline legs of the flows, in the direction the gas flows. Where the pipeline crosses the land border, a border metering station measures the gas, as at the interconnection points between real gas networks.

section.title: Specifications
section.para: Every document says which specification it follows. CustomizationID names a transaction: one kind of business message between two roles, with a purpose, a content and rules, as in CEN BII and Peppol. One or more document types carry a transaction (billing is the invoice, the credit note and the debit note), and one document type can carry several (an application response that answers an invoice is not one that answers a message). The specification has up to three levels, chained with #compliant# as EN 16931, Peppol and XRechnung chain theirs: the Trade Accord's transaction (urn:ubl-examples:world:trns:billing:1.0), a national specification built on it, such as Urvania's invoice rules for its value added tax or Bayvarra's rules for bills to its public bodies, and the specification of a community that exchanges among itself: the retail community of the distributor and the store, the port community of Lumeport, Urvania's energy market and public procurement. ProfileID names one of the Accord's generic process profiles (ordering, billing, transport, customs …), versioned, and no longer the flow; ProfileExecutionID identifies one collaboration under such a profile, given by the party that starts it (see "Document numbers"). Each specification has a short public page, and the build checks that every identifier a document uses has one. The world claims no compliance with real specifications such as EN 16931.

UBLVersionID gives the earliest UBL 2 version that defines every element the document uses, as its definition asks. The build computes it from the published models of UBL 2.0 to 2.5. For now every example needs 2.5: nearly all use elements that UBL 2.5 added, such as the electronic address and the further party identification.

section.title: Signatures
section.para: Signatures are to be redone as a stage of their own, after the stories of the flows are settled. The target is real electronic signatures, made and verified by the build. Which documents are signed, and how, is decided in that stage; until then the signatures in the examples stay as they are.

section.title: Who sends and who receives
section.para: Who sends and who receives a document type comes from the UBL 2.5 semantic model first: the elements SenderParty and ReceiverParty, or a definition of the document or of one of its party elements, such as "The Party who submits this Tender". Where the model does not say it, the party role table of the UBL specification is used. Where neither says it, the choice is marked as inferred, with the definitions it rests on. Every quote is checked word for word against its source.

section.title: Choosing and documenting values
section.para: Every value in an example document comes with the reason why it is that value. The reason is recorded where the value is made, and a document with a value without a reason is not built.

section.title: Where values come from
section.para: A value in an example comes from one of these sources, and its reason says which:

listitem.para: The world's layers. Party names, addresses, identifiers and accounts come from the identity of the party; items, their identifiers, customs tariff codes and prices from the items layer; currencies and tax rates from the countries layer. These values are the same in every document that uses them.

The structure of the flow. Which party sends the document, which receives it, and which other parties it names, at which place, come from the flow of documents, so the parties always sit where the business puts them.
The scenario of the flow. Document numbers, dates, quantities and the references between documents are what a flow adds; each carries its own reason, in business terms.
Code lists. Coded values come from the UBL default code lists or the world's own lists, and the reason names the list and the meaning of the code.

Calculation. Amounts are calculated from quantities and prices and rounded to the minor unit of the currency; the reason states the calculation. Every sum is stated in the document, as UBL requires, and never left to the receiver.

section.title: What a reason contains
section.para: A reason says why the value fits the element: what the element means in UBL, in this document, and what in the business situation makes this the value. It refers to the UBL definition and to the world's data first; a country rule or a specific process appears only as an illustration. For example, the quantity on an invoice for bulk ore is the weighed quantity from the despatch advice, not the ordered quantity, and its reason says so.

section.title: A party is described once per document
section.para: A party often plays several roles in one document: the buyer of an order is usually also its delivery party. Its full details (address, tax number, legal registration, contact, electronic address) are given once, at its first place in the document. Every later mention of the same party holds only its identifier and its name: enough to identify it, and never empty, as UBL requires (rule IND5). The same applies to a bank named more than once. The identifier is the party's number in its country's company register, given as PartyIdentification with the register as its scheme.

section.title: Only what UBL 2.5 endorses
section.para: The documents use only endorsed document types and elements, and they are validated against the schemas of the endorsed document types. Where UBL 2.5 replaced an element, the examples use the replacement: a party's electronic address, for instance, is carried in ElectronicAddress, because Party/EndpointID is deprecated.

section.title: Kept apart from the TC examples
section.para: The generated examples are kept in world/examples/, apart from the examples of the OASIS UBL Technical Committee in xml/, whose history is the base of this repository.

section.title: Checking the examples
section.para: The world is checked automatically every time the site is built. A build with a problem stops. The checks are layered like the world itself.

section.title: The world against the UBL 2.5 model
section.para: Every document in the world is checked against the UBL 2.5 semantic model:

listitem.para: every place where a party is mentioned exists in the structure of that document type;
every mandatory party element at document level is filled;
every party of the world takes part in at least one document.

section.title: Only what UBL 2.5 endorses
section.para: The examples use only document types, associations and properties that UBL 2.5 endorses. Anything the model marks as deprecated is rejected. A transport service, for example, is invoiced with the Invoice, because the Freight Invoice is deprecated.

section.title: Nothing empty, nothing implied
section.para: Two rules of the UBL specification shape the data the world needs:

listitem.para: No empty elements (IND5). A UBL document never contains an element without content: an aggregate needs a child, a basic element a value, and a value of only spaces counts as empty. Every party element must therefore hold at least one of its parts, even though none of them is mandatory in the schema. The identity of every party makes sure there is always something to put in it.

One text per language (IND7, IND8). Two sibling text elements of the same name never have the same languageID, and never both lack one. A text element repeats only to give the same text in another language, as the bilingual notes do; several keywords of an item therefore go in one search string. The text elements are the basic properties whose data type in the UBL 2.5 model is Text or Name: their schema types derive from the CCTS text type, which carries languageID.
No empty attributes (IND9). Every attribute that is present has a value.

An absence carries no meaning (IND6). Leaving an element out never says anything; the sender states every value that matters, and every sum (section 2.2.2, "Manifest Values"). An order without a carrier does not say that the seller arranges the transport: its delivery terms must say so. The world therefore requires values that would otherwise be implied, such as the delivery terms of every order.

section.title: The parties
section.para: The identity of every party is checked: every party has a name and every organisation an identifier; tax numbers and account numbers carry valid check digits; the city in the address is the nearest town or locality of the party's own country and state; every account is held at a bank of the world in the same country; and a bank named in a document is the bank where that party keeps its account. The ISIN of a listed company has the structure and check digit of ISO 6166 and starts with its country's code. Codana gives its company numbers in order of registration, each to one party, and every Codana identifier in a document starts with the number of the party that issued it. No identifier of a party repeats five digits of another, apart from the business register number in the electronic address and the customs trader number, and no telephone number repeats four digits of an identifier of its party.

section.title: The items
section.para: Units and packaging types must be codes of the UBL default lists; goods are identified in their maker's system: a GTIN under the prefix of the company that numbers them, which for a branded item is the brand owner, or on the Codana side KXU, the maker's company number and its own reference, at most 20 characters; every number is unique; prices are positive and in the seller's currency; gross weight is at least net weight. Every party that bills or offers in a document has items to put on its lines, and every party with items bills or offers them. The exchange rates between the currencies agree with each other.

section.title: The map and the code lists
section.para: The map is checked as a structure: one connected road network per landmass, houses on streets, nothing built on roads or water, believable terrain, and customs posts where roads cross a border.

The world's code lists are made from one source, world/codelists/lists.json, and the committed files must be what it makes. The country and currency lists hold exactly the codes of the countries layer. No invented code may be a real one: the currencies are checked against ISO 4217 and the market identifier codes against ISO 10383, both kept in world/codelists/sources. A copy of a real list may hold only codes that its source has.

section.title: The codes in the documents
section.para: The build gives every code its list. A code must be a code of its list, compared exactly, so en is not EN; the element gets the list's listID, and its reason says what the code means in the list. A text next to a code, such as CertificateType beside CertificateTypeCode, carries the list's name for the code. The build also checks what agrees between codes:

listitem.para: every allowance and charge has a reason code;
a tax exemption reason comes from the list of the seller's country;
a payment's clearing channel is one its payment system has, and the service level fits it (decision Q18);

the packing group and the packaging danger level of a UN number agree (I and 1, II and 2, III and 3, NA and 4), the hazardous category is the class, and an emergency card belongs to a class of the goods;
a size class follows from the company's headcount and turnover.

section.title: The example documents
section.para: The build checks that a reference to another document of the same flow quotes that document's UUID wherever it gives one. Every example document is validated in the two phases UBL prescribes:

listitem.para: Phase 1: against the UBL 2.5 runtime schema of its document type, from the endorsed set.

Phase 2: its coded values against the code lists, using context/value associations (CVA). It runs twice. First UBL's own phase 2, unchanged, with the UBL default code lists. The world replaces some of those lists, so this run may object only to values in their contexts: the countries and currencies, the lower-case languages, the allowance and charge codes, and the lists to which the world gives a listID. Then the world's own associations (world/codelists/UBL-World-2.5.cva), which replace UBL's: every code element must carry the listID of its list and a code of that list. An element with several meanings is bound by its parent element; an allowance by its ChargeIndicator (UN/EDIFACT 5189 for an allowance, 7161 or 5189 for a charge); where a context allows several lists, the listID chooses. A code element that no association covers is an error, unless it is a code a party defines for itself. The attributes are checked too: currencyID against the world's currencies, unitCode and mimeCode against UBL's lists, and languageID as a BCP 47 tag, a language of the world's ISO 639 list with an optional region.

section.para: The committed examples must also be up to date: they are generated again from the world's layers and compared, so a change in the world cannot leave an example behind.

section.title: Still to come
section.para: Later layers add their own checks: document lines with items and quantities, amounts and taxes that add up, dates in a believable order, references between documents, and quantities that agree from order to invoice. These apply to the example documents as they are generated for every flow.

ISO 4217: Codes for the representation of currencies; current list published by the maintenance agency, https://www.six-group.com/en/products-services/financial-information/data-standards.html.

RFC 2606: Reserved Top Level DNS Names (the .example domain), https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2606.

ISO/IEC 15459: the standard, in several parts, for unique identifiers issued under registered issuing agencies, under which Codana is an issuing agency and GS1 another.
ISO 8601: the standard for dates and times, whose week numbering and offsets from UTC the documents use.
ISO 11228-1: the standard on manual handling (lifting and carrying), whose limit of 25 kg for one person in good conditions the three countries apply.
WTO Valuation Agreement: the World Trade Organization's agreement on customs valuation (Articles 1 and 8), within which each country values its imports.
